newsitem.title: JAPAN: NTT to enter international phone market by end of 1997.
newsitem.headline: NTT to enter international phone market by end of 1997.

text.p: Japanese telecommunications giant NTT unveiled plans Wednesday for its long-awaited entry into the international telephone market, initially targeting conglomerates with offices around the world.

Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp. said it aimed to launch a special service later this year providing Japanese multinational corporations with telecommunications links between their offshoots in Europe, the United States and Asia.

This would be the first taste of the international phone business for NTT, the world's largest telecommunications company, after a 14-year wrangle with the government over its corporate structure and near-monopoly status in the domestic market.
The second stage of NTT's international strategy, after laws constricting its role are revised, will be to offer international phone services to the general public.

NTT said it was applying for licences in the United States and Asian countries as well as in Britain, Germany and France to operate its new corporate service. It did not specify the likely scale of the investment needed to launch the service.
"We hope to be able to start the service in such regions by the end of this year," NTT president Junichiro Miyazu told a news conference.

"The initial target would be Japanese multinationals, but we hope to provide broader and more comprehensive services for individual customers in the second stage," he said, without giving a timeframe for the proposed expansion.
Under the "NTT Global Service," multinational conglomerates will be able to send voice and data messages along international telephone lines to their group companies.
NTT will also help the multinationals construct in-house computer networks, an NTT spokesman said.
NTT's entry into the business is expected to fuel competition with overseas carriers providing similar services.

International carriers British Telecommunications Plc and MCI Communications Corp. are seeking a tie-up between NTT and their joint venture Concert to boost the credibility of their own corporate link-up service in the Asia-Pacific region.
Miyazu said NTT may enter into alliances with other international carriers as it expands into the global marketplace, but declined to elaborate on possible partners.
He said regulatory barriers would restrict the range of its international services for the time being, but those obstacles should soon be removed.

NTT will not be able to include Japan in its international telecommunications loop until the law on its status is formally revised in the middle of this year, he said. The law will be discussed in a parliamentary session starting later this month.

NTT has long sought to break into the lucrative international market but its entry has been delayed by wrangling with the government over whether the giant company should be broken up into smaller entities to generate greater competition and efficiency.

Under a compromise announced in early December, NTT will be broken up into a set of companies under the wing of a holding company. One of the companies will be allowed to operate international services.
